reader_questions.q: How large is France’s debt relative to its economy, how has that burden changed, and what evidence establishes whether this is a crisis rather than a persistent fiscal problem?
reader_questions.where: Opening paragraphs and france-debt-crisis-debt.svg establish the scale and history; the final substantive paragraph explicitly sets aside market and political crisis evidence unavailable in these data.

reader_questions.q: How does France’s annual deficit compare with its own past and with Germany, Italy, Spain and the EU overall?
reader_questions.where: “The gap has never closed” gives historical comparisons; “Not a low-tax country” and france-debt-crisis-vs-eu.svg give all requested peer comparisons for 2025.

reader_questions.q: How much of the deterioration in France’s finances reflects higher spending versus weaker revenue relative to GDP, and when did the main shifts occur?
reader_questions.where: “The gap has never closed” quantifies spending and revenue changes since 2019 and explains the 2025 improvement; the earlier major deteriorations are labelled but not decomposed.

reader_questions.q: Is France borrowing mainly to pay interest on existing debt, or does its spending exceed revenue even before interest costs?
reader_questions.where: “The interest bill is growing fast” gives the 2025 deficit excluding interest as 2.9% of GDP, against a total deficit of 5.1%.

reader_questions.q: Which public services and benefits account for the largest spending shares, and which have contributed most to the increase in spending relative to GDP?
reader_questions.where: “Not a low-tax country” identifies economic types behind the spending difference from the EU and cites pensions’ contribution to nominal spending growth in 2024; it does not rank spending purposes or their changes relative to GDP.

reader_questions.q: Has the debt burden kept rising outside periods of sharp fiscal deterioration, and how does its path in euros differ from its path relative to GDP?
reader_questions.where: france-debt-crisis-debt.svg shows the longer trajectory; “The gap has never closed” explains the 2021–23 ratio decline despite rising euro debt and the renewed rise despite the 2025 deficit improvement.

reader_questions.q: How large a spending reduction or revenue increase would close the latest annual deficit, and how much of that gap would remain if interest costs were excluded?
reader_questions.where: The peer-comparison and interest sections supply 5.1% and 2.9% of GDP, but leave the reader to translate these into the required adjustment and omit the corresponding euro amounts.

missed_findings: The available functional accounts could identify the largest public services and benefits and their contributions to spending growth relative to GDP; the outline itself identifies social protection at 23.7% of GDP in 2024, including old age at 13.4%, but the prose omits both.
Cash benefits and public pay explain much of France’s spending premium over the EU, but the story does not unpack the benefits or show which components increased or declined over time.
Revenue fell from 54.3% of GDP in 2017 to 52.1% in 2025, providing an earlier starting point for the revenue weakening than the prose’s 2019 comparison.

Closing the 2025 deficit would require an accounting adjustment of about €153bn, or 5.1% of GDP, with about €86bn, or 2.9% of GDP, still required excluding interest, before allowing for economic feedback.
The annual spending and revenue series could separate their contributions to the earlier deficit spikes rather than leaving those episodes as unexplained landmarks.

charts.glance: France’s debt burden has roughly doubled since 2000, with a temporary retreat after 2021 followed by a new high.
charts.encodings: The solid blue line represents gross debt relative to GDP, identified by the title and axis label; equal-sized filled red circles mark directly labelled observations, and red endpoint text emphasizes the latest value.
charts.shows: Quarterly gross debt relative to GDP, selected euro debt levels, and a textual comparison of cumulative deficits with the debt increase.
charts.fix: Use a takeaway title stating that the debt ratio nearly doubled; the current title only names the measure.

charts.glance: Government spending stays above revenue throughout, with especially wide gaps around 2009 and 2020.
charts.encodings: The solid dark line is spending and the solid blue line revenue, both directly labelled; pale red shading represents the deficit, explicitly explained on the chart; matching filled dots mark the labelled 2019 observations.
charts.shows: Annual spending and revenue relative to GDP and the persistent gap between them, including the latest narrowing.

charts.glance: France’s spending exceeds the EU benchmark by more than its revenue does, with benefits and employee pay the largest named spending differences.
charts.encodings: Bar length and direction encode France minus the EU in GDP percentage points; dark bars are totals, blue bars positive spending components, and grey the negative component. Row labels and signed values make the quantities readable, but the total/component colour hierarchy is only implicit; colour also repeats the sign encoding.
charts.shows: The spending and revenue premiums over the EU, a breakdown of the spending premium, and two additional peer comparisons in small caption text.
charts.fix: Separate and label the totals and spending-component blocks so readers immediately see that the lower bars explain the spending total.

charts.glance: The nominal interest bill has climbed sharply since 2021 to its highest level in the displayed period.
charts.encodings: Equal-width bars encode annual interest payments through height; grey represents 1995–2020 and red 2021–25, but no legend explains that colour boundary. Selected labels give euro amounts and GDP shares; red text also emphasizes the latest value and the deficit excluding interest.
charts.shows: Interest payments in current euros, with selected GDP-share comparisons and a separate note on the deficit excluding interest.
charts.fix: Label the red interval explicitly as 2021–25, the period over which the interest bill nearly doubled.

top_change: Add a compact spending-by-function explanation showing the largest services and benefits and their contributions to the increase relative to GDP, including the components of social protection; make room by shortening the production notes.

lessons.rule: When spending is central to an explanation, show what its largest categories contain and which components changed.
lessons.evidence: Cash benefits and employee pay explain the EU premium, but the available functional accounts are not used to explain the domestic spending increase.

lessons.rule: Distinguish a cross-sectional difference from a contribution to change over time.
lessons.evidence: The EU spending comparison and pensions’ contribution to nominal growth do not answer which services drove the increase in spending relative to GDP.

lessons.rule: Translate a deficit into the adjustment the reader is asking about, rather than leaving the arithmetic implicit.
lessons.evidence: The story gives total and interest-excluding deficits as GDP shares but never states the corresponding €153bn and €86bn gaps.

lessons.rule: Make colour groupings explicit on the chart even when the underlying values are labelled.
lessons.evidence: The comparison chart’s total/component hierarchy and the interest chart’s red time interval lack explicit keys.

lessons.rule: Use the measure that matches the claim, especially when comparing taxation with broader government revenue.
lessons.evidence: “Not a low-tax country” is supported with total revenue, which the story itself correctly says includes sales as well as taxes and contributions.

argument.why: The title and early accounting comparison establish a clear explanation through persistent deficits, and every substantive section serves it within the acknowledged data limits.

depth.why: The accounting mechanism, peer benchmarks and interest alternative are useful, but the largest spending categories and their contributions to change remain insufficiently unpacked.

charts.why: All four support the prose, but the comparison chart combines several points and both bar charts leave colour groupings implicit.

honesty.why: Sources, crisis limitations and the interest-definition disagreement are disclosed, but the tax heading relies on broader revenue and the 2019–25 component changes are not reconciled with rounded deficit figures.

reader_questions.why: Debt, deficit comparisons and interest are answered well; spending purposes, the full spending/revenue decomposition and the required adjustment remain partial.

prose.why: The main prose is mostly plain and figures are contextualized with GDP, but the lengthy production notes add padding and terms such as “benefits in kind bought in” remain unexplained.
